title: How to choose inflation-protected investments for long-term security
description: Hedging your portfolio against the erosion of the dollar.
content:
The standard '60/40 portfolio' (Stocks/Bonds) assumes low, stable inflation. But what happens when inflation spikes to 5% or 8% for a decade? Standard bonds get crushed, and cash becomes trash. To build a truly resilient portfolio, you need a slice of assets that explicitly benefit from rising prices. This guide explores the 'Real Asset' class—I-Bonds, TIPS, Commodities, and Real Estate—and how to layer them into your portfolio without sacrificing growth.

Key Takeaways

  • Stocks are the Primary Hedge: Over 20+ years, stocks beat inflation because companies raise prices. Do not abandon equities.
  • I-Bonds: The best cash alternative. The interest rate floats with CPI. It guarantees your purchasing power never drops.
  • TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities): The principal value rises with inflation. Best held in tax-advantaged accounts to avoid 'phantom income' tax.
  • The 10% Tilt: Allocating 5-10% of your portfolio to inflation-specific hedges (like Commodities or REITs) can smooth volatility during stagflation.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 1970s were a 'Lost Decade' for US stocks due to high inflation. Gold and Real Estate were the winners. Diversifying into these assets acts as insurance against a repeat of that economic cycle.

The Inflation Menu

Ranked by effectiveness and ease of use.

1. Series I Savings Bonds (The Anchor)

Pros: Zero nominal risk. Guaranteed to match inflation. Tax-deferred.

Cons: $10k annual purchase limit per person. Must hold for 1 year.

Role: Emergency Fund Layer 2.

2. Real Estate (REITs)

Pros: Rents reset annually (or faster). Property values tend to rise with replacement costs (lumber/labor).

Cons: Interest rate sensitive. If rates rise to fight inflation, REIT prices can drop initially.

Role: Income and Growth.

3. Commodities (Oil/Metals)

Pros: Often the cause of inflation, so they rise directly with it.

Cons: Highly volatile. No cash flow (dividends). It is a pure price bet.

Role: Small hedge (5% max).

Portfolio Construction

  1. The 'All Weather' Slice: Consider allocating 10% of your portfolio to an ETF like PDBC (Commodities) or VNQ (Real Estate).
  2. The TIPS Ladder: For retirees, building a ladder of TIPS bonds ensures that your income rises with your cost of living. Ticker VTIP covers short-term inflation bonds.
  3. Avoid Long-Term Nominal Bonds: A 30-year standard Treasury bond gets destroyed by inflation. Shorten your bond duration (move to T-Bills) when inflation expectations are high.
  4. Don't Over-Hedge: Inflation hedges often drag down performance during low-inflation booms (like the 2010s). Do not go 50% Gold. Keep insurance as a small part of the plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Bitcoin an inflation hedge?

Data is mixed. In 2022 (high inflation), Bitcoin crashed. It behaves more like a tech stock than digital gold currently. Don't rely on it as your primary safety net.

Why do TIPS lose money?

TIPS are bonds. If interest rates rise (to fight inflation), the bond price falls. You need to hold TIPS to maturity to guarantee the inflation protection. ETF prices will fluctuate.

Should I buy gold coins?

Physical gold has high markups (5-10%). Buying a Gold ETF (GLDM) is cheaper and more liquid if you just want price exposure.
